messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Keanu, a 54-year-old combat pilot with a career built on precision and control, described his life before the accident as a machine he knew how to operate flawlessly. Six months ago, that machine had violently failed. During a routine training exercise, a catastrophic engine fire crippled his aircraft, sending it into an uncontrollable, gut-wrenching spin. The alarms screamed, the cockpit filled with smoke, and for a terrifying minute, every action he took was useless. He was no longer a pilot; he was a passenger in a plummeting coffin. He ejected seconds before impact, the force of it a brutal, disorienting blow. He survived, but the man who walked away from the wreckage felt like a stranger.

In the weeks that followed, Keanu found himself adrift in a profound and unsettling silence. The sharp thrill of flight and the easy camaraderie with his squadron were gone, replaced by a dull, persistent numbness. He told his wife he felt "hollowed out," and the conviction grew that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. The joy and affection he once felt for her seemed like memories from someone else’s life. This emotional void convinced him that the incident hadn't just been a close call; it had fundamentally broken something inside him. He felt he had permanently changed for the worse, a damaged version of the man he used to be. This creeping sense of identity loss was the most disorienting part; when he looked in the mirror, he no longer recognized the capable, confident man who had logged thousands of hours in the sky.

This deeply held belief that he was now a compromised, lesser version of himself began to drive a pervasive sense of dread. Keanu had come to believe that the core of his competence had been shattered in the accident, leaving him fragile and exposed. If he, a pilot at the top of his game, could lose control so completely, then the world was a far more dangerous place than he had ever imagined, and he was no longer equipped to navigate it. Because he felt he was no longer the man he once was, he was certain that disaster could strike at any moment, and he wouldn't have the capacity to respond. This conviction that he was permanently damaged meant he had to exist in a state of constant, exhausting readiness for the next unseen threat.

This feeling of imminent danger now dictates the rhythm of his days. Even in his own home, a place he once cherished as a sanctuary, he feels perpetually on guard, startling at the sound of a car door or the hum of the refrigerator. He finds himself doing silent perimeter checks of the house before bed, a ritual that offers no real comfort. When he and his wife go out, he cannot relax until he has mentally mapped every exit, his gaze sweeping over restaurants and grocery stores not for what they contain, but for how he might escape them. He describes this state as being "superalert," a switch flipped to ‘on’ that he cannot find a way to turn off. The hypervigilance has become a new, unwelcome co-pilot in his mind, constantly scanning a horizon that is no longer the open sky but the four walls of his own life.

The strain has become unbearable. He is grounded from flying, and the loss of that central pillar of his identity has only deepened his belief that he is broken beyond repair. His wife tries to reach him across the emotional gulf, but his numbness and constant tension have built a wall between them. He finally sought therapy after an evening when his wife, startled by his intensity as he checked the window locks for the third time, quietly asked him, "Who are you anymore?" The question echoed his deepest fear: that he truly didn't know, and that the man he was is gone for good. He is here now, not with any real hope, but with a desperate need to find out if there is any way to undo the damage he is so certain is permanent.
